entities.name: Verrius Flaccus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Verrius Flaccus (d. 20 CE) was a preeminent Roman grammarian, philologist, and antiquarian whose encyclopedic scholarship profoundly influenced the systematization of Latin language and culture during the Augustan and early Tiberian eras. Flourishing under the patronage of Emperor Augustus, who entrusted him with the education of his grandsons Gaius and Lucius Caesar, Flaccus played a critical role in standardizing Roman linguistic and historical knowledge, shaping the intellectual landscape of the nascent Roman Empire. His work was foundational for later lexicography and classical studies, establishing a high benchmark for scholarly rigor in the Roman world.

Flaccus's most monumental achievement was the *De verborum significatu* ('On the Meaning of Words'), an immense lexical and antiquarian dictionary that originally spanned many books. Though this colossal work is lost, its extensive epitome by Sextus Pompeius Festus in the 2nd century CE, and later by Paul the Deacon in the 8th century, preserves fragments of its unparalleled scope. This dictionary systematically cataloged archaic Latin words, their etymologies, grammatical forms, and historical usage, drawing upon a vast array of earlier Roman authors and historical records. He also authored *Fasti Praenestini*, a calendar inscribed on marble tablets in Praeneste, detailing Roman festivals and their historical origins, providing invaluable insight into Roman religious practices and chronology.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Verrius Flaccus's monumental lexicographical and antiquarian works, though largely preserved through epitomes, systematized and transmitted core Roman linguistic and cultural knowledge. His efforts profoundly influenced subsequent classical scholarship and served as a vital link for understanding ancient Rome into the Middle Ages.
